Hu Li: It's going to rain.
Master Dong: Indeed, it's going to rain. I've heard that foxes in their dens can sense the wind rising, and mice in their holes can foresee the rain coming. It seems you must be either a fox or a mouse.
Hu Li: You know me?
Master Dong: No, but I've been waiting for you—waiting for you to come and kill me.
Hu Li: Aren't you afraid of death?
Master Dong: No, I am afraid of death, but there are things I fear more than death. The same goes for you, Master, isn't it?
Hu Li: Oh? Then what do you fear?
Master Dong: Master, though I follow Confucianism, I have also studied the teachings of the Hundred Schools.
Hu Li: Why?
Master Dong: Because I sought a great path—one that could bring true peace to the world.
Master Dong: I once studied Legalism, but the First Emperor ruled the land with harsh laws, wielding the whip to subdue all under heaven. Though his might shook the four seas, the people never found contentment.
Master Dong: Later, I turned to Daoism, but in the early Han, governance by the principles of Huang-Lao let the people roam like wild horses, without guidance, and the powerful never restrained themselves.
Master Dong: I also learned Mohism, but Mohists preach universal love and non-aggression, rejecting human bonds and sacrificing oneself for others. How many in this world could truly follow such ideals?
Hu Li: So you believe that among the Hundred Schools, only Confucianism holds the true great path?
Master Dong: Confucianism... is not it either.
Hu Li: Then, what is the path you seek?
Master Dong: I once had a dream—a vision of the world two thousand years hence.
Master Dong: There, Confucianism formed the backbone, upholding the anthem of ages; Mohism served as the blade, protecting all living beings; Legalism set the measure, balancing all things. The Hundred Schools converged into one, and the hearts of the people were united. There was no fear of famine, nor suffering from chaos.
Hu Li: You wish to merge the Hundred Schools! Aren't you afraid of being scorned by the Confucian Gate?
Master Dong: Earlier, you asked me what I fear. Now I can answer. I fear... that this is just a dream.
Master Dong: Morning mushrooms know not the waxing and waning of the moon; cicadas understand not the passing of seasons. One who has never seen mountains cannot fathom the flatness of the earth, and one who has beheld the vast sea cannot return to tiny streams.
Master Dong: Ten years may plan for a dynasty's rise and fall; a hundred years may plan for the shift of power; a thousand years may plan for the continuity of culture. Master, you and I stand in this eternal torrent—why not gaze across the millennia and strive for a legacy of ten thousand years?
Hu Li: What do you intend to do?
Master Dong: To bring peace to the world, we must unify the Hundred Schools under the Kingly Way, and this will inevitably clash with Mohist universal love.
Master Dong: Thus, I shamelessly propose to borrow a thousand years from the Mohists on behalf of the world. For the next two millennia, let one thousand belong to Confucianism and one thousand to Mohism. Only then can true harmony be achieved.
……………………
Hu Li: How do you plan to borrow it?
Master Dong: I ask the Mohists to die.
